¶
'''wavelet''' (wāv′let), ''n.'' [< ''wave''<sup>1</sup> + ''-let.''] A small wave; a ripple.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like the vague sighings of a wind at even,
That wakes the ''wavelets'' of the slumbering sea.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Queen Mab, viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The head, with its thin ''wavelets'' of brown hair, indents the little pillow.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Amos Barton, ii.}}}}

'''wave-line''' (wāv′līn), ''n.'' '''1.''' The outline of a wave; specifically, in ''physics'', the path of a wave of light, sound, etc., or the graphic representation of such a path.—'''2.''' ''Naut.'', the general outline of the surface of sea-waves: specifically used attributively to note a method of ship-building devised by J. Scott Russell, in which the lines of the hull of a vessel are adapted scientifically to the lines of the waves, and are nearly or quite cycloidal.—'''3.''' One of the series of lines or furrows produced by the sea-waves upon a sandy beach.

'''wavellite''' (wā′vel-īt), ''n.'' [Named after William ''Wavell'', an English medical practitioner (died 1829), by whom it was discovered.] A hydrous phosphate of aluminium, commonly found in radiated hemispherical or globular crystalline concretions from a very small size to 1 inch in diameter, and of a white to yellow-green or brown color. See cut under ''radiate.''

'''wave-loaf''' (wāv′lōf), ''n.'' A loaf for a wave-offering.
{{smaller block|Ye shall bring out of your habitations two ''wave loaves'' of two tenth deals.
{{right|Lev. xxiii. 17.}}}}

In ''bot.'', undate.—'''4.''' In ''her.'', same as ''undé.''—{{smaller|'''Waved sandpiper†.''' See ''sandpiper.''—'''Waved sword.''' In ''her.'', a flamboyant sword used as a bearing.—'''Waved wheel.''' See ''wheel''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''wave-front''' (wāv′frunt), ''n.'' The continuous line or surface including all the particles in the same phase. It is a spherical surface for sound, and for light in an isotropic medium.

'''wave-goose''' (wāv′gös), ''n.'' The brant- or brent-goose, ''Bernicla brenta.'' [Durham, Eng.]

'''wave-length''' (wāv′length), ''n.'' The distance between the crests of two adjacent waves, or between the lowest parts of the depressions on each side of a wave; more generally, the distance between any particle of the disturbed medium and the next which is in the same phase with it. See ''wave''<sup>1</sup>, 3.
{{smaller block|The ''wave-length'' of a ray of light in any given substance is consequently obtained by dividing the ''wave-length'' in air by the index of refraction of the substance itself.
{{right|''Lommel'', Light (trans.), p. 245.}}}}
{{smaller block|No difference but that of ''wave-length'' is recognized between waves of radiant heat and of radiant light.
{{right|''Sci. Amer. Supp.'', p. 8801.}}}}

'''waveless''' (wāv′les), ''a.''   [< ''wave''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.'']   Free from waves; undisturbed; unagitated; still.
{{smaller block|Smoother than this ''waveless'' spring.
{{right|''Peele'', David and Bethsabe.}}}}
{{smaller block|The mist that sleeps on a ''waveless'' sea.
{{right|''Hogg'', Kilmeny.}}}}
{{smaller block|Unmoved the bannered blazonry hung ''waveless'' as a pall.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, II. iii.}}}}

'''wavelet''' (wāv′let), ''n.''   [< ''wave''<sup>1</sup> + ''-let.'']   A small wave; a ripple.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like the vague sighings of a wind at even,
That wakes the ''wavelets'' of the slumbering sea.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Queen Mab, viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The head, with its thin ''wavelets'' of brown hair, indents the little pillow.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Amos Barton, ii.}}}}

'''wave-line''' (wāv′līn), ''n.'' '''1.''' The outline of a wave; specifically, in ''physics'', the path of a wave of light, sound, etc., or the graphic representation of such a path.—'''2.''' ''Naut.'', the general outline of the surface of sea-waves: specifically used attributively to note a method of ship-building devised by J. Scott Russell, in which the lines of the hull of a vessel are adapted scientifically to the lines of the waves, and are nearly or quite cycloidal.—'''3.''' One of the series of lines or furrows produced by the sea-waves upon a sandy beach.

'''wavellite''' (wā′vel-īt), ''n.''   [Named after William ''Wavell'', an English medical practitioner (died 1829), by whom it was discovered.]   A hydrous phosphate of aluminium, commonly found in radiated hemispherical or globular crystalline concretions from a very small size to 1 inch in diameter, and of a white to yellow-green or brown color. See cut under ''radiate.''

'''wave-loaf''' (wāv′lōf), ''n.'' A loaf for a wave-offering.
{{smaller block|Ye shall bring out of your habitations two ''wave loaves'' of two tenth deals.
{{right|Lev. xxiii. 17.}}}}

'''wave-molding''' (wāv′mōl″ding), ''n.'' In ''arch.'', a molding of undulating outline, resembling more or less closely a succession of waves; particularly, a molding of Greek origin, much used in Renaissance and modern architecture, having the character of a series of breaking waves, much conventionalized.

'''wave-motion''' (wāv′mō″shọn), ''n.'' Motion in curves alternately concave and convex like that of the waves of the sea; undulatory motion. See ''wave''<sup>1</sup>, 3.
{{smaller block|While ether-waves are in course of traversing the ether, there is neither heat, light, nor chemical decomposition; merely ''wave-motion'', and transference of energy by ''wave-motion''. {{right|''A. Daniell'', Prin. of Physics, p. 434.}}}}
{{smaller block|The essential characteristic of ''wave-motion'' is that a disturbance of some kind is handed on from one portion of a solid or fluid mass to another. {{right|''P. G. Tait'', Encyc. Brit., XIV. 603.}}}}

'''wave-offering''' (wāv′of″ėr-ing), ''n.'' In the ancient Jewish law, an offering presented with a horizontal movement of the hands forward and backward and toward the right and left, whereas the heave-offering was elevated and lowered.

'''wave-path''' (wāv′päth), ''n.'' The line along which any point in any wave is propagated. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The radial lines along which an earthquake may be propagated from the centrum are called ''wave-paths''. {{right|''J. Milne'', Earthquakes, p. 9.}}}}

'''waver'''<sup>1</sup> (wā′vėr), ''v.''   [< ME. ''waveren'', ''wayveren'', vacillate, < AS. as if *''wafrian'' (cf. ''wæfre'', wavering, wandering, restless: said of flame and fire, the mind or spirit, etc.) = MHG. ''waberen'', G. dial. ''wabern'', waver, totter, move to and fro, = Icel. ''vafra'', hover about, = Norw. ''vavra'', flap about; also, with var. suffix, MHG. ''wabelen'', webelen'', fluctuate, waver, = Icel. ''vafla'', hover about (see ''wabble''<sup>1</sup>); freq. of the verb represented by ''wave''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To move up and down or to and fro; wave; float; flutter; be tossed or rocked about; sway.
{{smaller block|<poem>All in wer for to walt, ''wayuerande'' he sote,
But he held hym on horse, houyt o lofte.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8266.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For an Outlawe, this is the Lawe,
  That Men hym take and binde,
Without pytee, hanged to bee,
  And ''waver'' with the Wynde.</poem>
{{right|''The Nut-Brown Maid'', quoted by Prior (Poems, [ed. 1756, I. 147).}}}}
{{smaller block|The wind in his raiment ''wavered.''
{{right|''William Morris'', Sigurd, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To quiver; flicker; glimmer; glance.
{{smaller block|<poem>As when a sunbeam ''wavers'' warm
Within the dark and dimpled beck.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Miller’s Daughter.}}}}
'''3.''' To falter; fail; reel; totter.
{{smaller block|<poem>Keep my wits, Heaven! I feel ’em ''wavering'';
Oh God, my head!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Pilgrim, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|How many ''wavering'' steps can we retrace in our past lives!
{{right|''Channing'', Perfect Life, p. 74.}}}}
{{smaller block|Like the day of doom it seemed to her ''wavering'' senses.
{{right|''Longfellow'', Evangeline, i. 5.}}}}
'''4.''' To be undetermined or irresolute; fluctuate; vacillate.
{{smaller block|Therefore be sure, and ''waver'' not of God’s love and favour towards you in Christ.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 132.}}}}
{{smaller block|He that ''wavereth'' is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
{{right|Jas. i. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|I expect you should sollicit me as much as if I were ''wavering'' at the Grate of a Monastery, with one Foot over the Threshold. {{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1 and 4.''' ''Vacillate.'' See ''fluctuate.''—'''4.''' ''Hesitate'', etc. See ''scruple.''}}

'''II.'''† ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to wave or move to and fro; set in waving motion; brandish.
{{smaller block|Item, if the Admirall shall happen to hull in the night, then to make a wauering light ouer his other light, ''wauering'' the light vpon a pole. {{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', III. 147.}}}}
'''2.''' To demur or scruple about; hesitate at; shirk.
{{smaller block|<poem>The inconstant Barons ''wavering'' every hour
The fierce encounter of this boist’rous tide
That easily might her livelihood devour.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Barons’ Wars, i. 34.}}}}

'''waver'''<sup>2</sup> (wā′vėr), ''n.''   [< ''wave''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who or that which waves; specifically, in ''printing'', an inking-roller; an apparatus which distributes ink on the table or on other rollers, but not on the form of types: so called from its vibratory movement.
{{smaller block|As the carriage returns, this strip of ink is distributed on the inking table by rollers placed diagonally across the machine. The diagonal position gives them a waving motion; hence they are called ''wavers.'' {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 706.}}}}

'''waver'''<sup>3</sup> (wā′vėr), ''n.''   [Perhaps < ''wave''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup> (?).]   A sapling or timberling left standing in a fallen wood. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|As you pass along, prune and trim up all the young ''wavers.'' {{right|''Evelyn'', Sylva, III. i. 7.}}}}

'''waver-dragon''' (wā′vėr-drag″on), ''n.''   [< ''waver'' for ''wiver'' + ''dragon''.]   In ''her.'', the wivern.

'''waverer''' (wā′vėr-ėr), ''n.''   [< ''waver''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who or that which wavers or fluctuates; especially, a person who vacillates or is undecided in mind.
{{smaller block|Come, young ''waverer'', come, go with me.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 3. 89.}}}}
{{smaller block|This prospect of converting votes was a dangerous distraction to Mr. Brooke; his impression that ''waverers'' were likely to be allured by wavering statements . . . gave Will Ladislaw much trouble. {{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, li.}}}}

'''waveringly''' (wā′vėr-ing-li), ''n.'' In a wavering, vacillating, or irresolute manner.
{{smaller block|Loke not ''wauueringly'' about you, haue no distrust, be not afrayd. {{right|''J. Udall'', On 1 Pet. v.}}}}

'''waveringness''' (wā′vėr-ing-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of a waverer; vacillation.
{{smaller block|The ''waveringness'' of our cupidities turneth the minde into a diziness unawares to itself.
{{right|''W. Montague'', Devoute Essays, Pref.}}}}

'''waver-roller''' (wâ′vėr-rō″lėr), ''n.'' In ''printing'', a roller made to vibrate in a diagonal direction on the inking-table of a printing-machine for the purpose of distributing the ink.

'''wavery''' (wā′vėr-i), ''a.''   [< ''waver''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Wavering; unsteady; shaky; faltering.
{{smaller block|Old letters closely covered with a ''wavery'' writing.
{{right|''Miss Thackeray'', Book of Sibyls, p. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|He’s . . . ''wavery''; . . . his love changes like the seasons. {{right|''Christian Union'', July 28, 1887.}}}}

'''wave-shell''' (wāv′shel), ''n.'' In earthquake-shocks, one of the waves of alternate compression and expansion, having theoretically the form of concentric shells, which are propagated in all directions through the solid materials of the earth’s crust from the seismic focus to the earth’s surface. ''Encyc. Brit.'', VII. 610.

'''waveson''' (wāv′sọn), ''n.''   [Appar. irreg. < ''wave''<sup>2</sup>, ''waive'', + ''-son'', after the analogy of ''flotson'', ''jetson'', ''jettison'', otherwise ''flotsam'', ''jetsam''.]   A name given to goods which after a shipwreck appear floating on the sea.

'''wave-surface''' (wāv′sėr″fās), ''n.'' A surface whose equation in rectangular coördinates is
{{block center|<math>x^2/(1-\mathrm{A}^2r^2)+y^2/(1-\mathrm{B}^2r^2)+z^2/(1-\mathrm{C}^2r^2)=0.</math>}}
{{smaller block|If upon every central section of a quadric surface be erected a perpendicular at the center, and points be taken on this perpendicular at distances from the center equal to the axes of the section, then the locus of these points will be the wave-surface. It is frequently called ''Fresnel’s wave-surface'', to distinguish it from ''Huygens’s wave-surface'', which is simply an ellipsoid—the latter being the form of the wave-front of a uniaxial crystal, the former that of a biaxial crystal.—'''Malus’s wave-surface''' [discovered by E. L. ''Malus'' (1775–1812) in 1810], a surface of the wave-front of light emanating from a point but undergoing reflections and refractions at different surfaces.}}

'''wave-trap''' (wāv′trap), ''n.'' In ''hydraulic engin.'', a widening inward of the spaces between piers, to afford space to permit waves rolling in between the piers to lose force by spreading themselves.

'''wave-worn''' (wāv′wōrn), ''a.'' Worn by the waves.
{{smaller block|The shore that o’er his ''wave-worn'' basis bow’d. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 1. 120.}}}}

'''wavey, wavy<sup>2</sup>''' (wâ′vi), ''n.''; pl. ''waveys, wavies'' (-viz).   [From Amer. Ind. name ''wawa''.]   A goose of the genus ''Chen''; a snow-goose.

{{smaller block|Shooting ''Wavies'' on the little lakes with which this region [the Red River country] is dotted is said to be a favorite amusement of the sportsmen.
{{right|''Sportsman’s Gazetteer'', p. 192.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Blue wavey,''' the blue-winged goose, ''Chen cærulescens.''—'''Horned wavey,''' the smallest snow-goose, ''Chen'' (''Exanthemops'') ''rossi'', which has at times the base of the bill studded with tubercles. It is exactly like the snow-goose in plumage, but no larger than a mallard, and inhabits}}
{{smaller|arctic America, coming southward in migration. It was recognizably described under its present name by Hearne, but lost sight of for nearly a century, till brought again to notice, in 1861, by J. Cassin.—'''White wavey,''' the snow-goose. See cut under ''Chen''.}}

[[File:century v08 p0656 c3f1.png|center|145px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Horned Wavey (''Chen rossi'').}}}}

'''wavily''' (wā′vi-li), ''adv.'' In a wavy manner, form, or direction.
{{smaller block|Mr. Rappit, the hair-dresser, with his well-anointed coronal locks tending ''wavily'' upward.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 9.}}}}

'''waviness''' (wā′vi-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being wavy or undulating.

'''waving-frame''' (wā′ving-frām), ''n.'' In ''printing'', a frame which carries inking-rollers.
{{smaller block|The frame which supports the inking-rollers, called the ''waving-frame'', is attached by hinges to the general framework of the machine; the edge of the stereotype-plate cylinder is indented, and rubs against the ''waving-frame'', causing it to vibrate to and fro, and consequently to carry the inking-rollers with it, so as to give them an unceasing traverse motion. {{right|''Ure'', Dict., III. 655.}}}}

'''wavy'''<sup>1</sup> (wā′vi), ''a.''   [< ''wave''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Abounding in waves.
{{smaller block|This said, she div’d into the ''wavy'' seas.
{{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey, iv. 569.}}}}
'''2.''' Undulating in movement or shape; waving: as, ''wavy'' hair.
{{smaller block|Let her glad Vallies smile with ''wavy'' Corn.
{{right|''Prior'', Carmen Seculare (1700), st. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''wavy'' swell of the soughing reeds.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Dying Swan.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''bot.'', undulating on the border or on the surface. See cut under ''repand''.—'''4.''' In ''her.'', same as ''undé''.—'''5.''' In ''entom.'', presenting a series of horizontal curves: noting marks or margins. It is distinct from ''waved''; but the two epithets are somewhat loosely used, and are sometimes interchanged.—'''6.''' In ''zoöl.'', undulating; sinuous; waved; having waved markings.—'''Barry wavy.''' {{smaller|See ''barry''<sup>2</sup>.}}—'''Sword wavy.''' {{smaller|See ''sword''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Wavy respiration.''' {{smaller|Same as ''interrupted respiration'' (which see, under ''respiration'').}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
